one_liner: Header-only C++11 HAT-trie string map/set using about 3x less memory than std::unordered_map<std::string, T>.
what_it_does: tsl::htrie_map<char, T> and tsl::htrie_set<char> store a large dynamic set of strings (or string-to-value map) compactly and add prefix queries: equal_prefix_range, erase_prefix, longest_prefix and for_each_prefix_of, plus serialize/deserialize. The interface resembles std::unordered_map (insert, emplace, find, at, operator[], erase, count) but keys are passed as const char* plus length, std::string or std::string_view, and there is no std::string key object: it.key() rebuilds the key into a string on demand. Only char keys are supported (a static_assert rejects other character types); UTF-8 and binary keys with embedded NULs work.
how_it_is_fast: It implements the HAT-trie of Askitis and Sinha (2007): a burst trie whose leaves are cache-conscious array hash tables (Askitis and Zobel 2005). Each array-hash bucket is one malloc'd contiguous buffer of [2-byte length][key bytes][value index] records, so a lookup hashes the key suffix and scans one short buffer instead of chasing a pointer per entry, and no per-key heap node or 32-byte std::string header is stored; values sit in a separate std::vector indexed by a 16-bit position. When a leaf reaches burst_threshold entries (16384 by default) it bursts into a trie node (a 256-entry child-pointer array) keyed on the first character, so common prefixes are stored once. The default max_load_factor of 8 entries per bucket favors memory; lowering it buys faster reads for more memory.
when_to_use: Millions to hundreds of millions of string keys (titles, URLs, words, paths) where std::unordered_map<std::string, T> memory is the problem: the README shows 402 MiB vs 1247 MiB on 13.1M Wikipedia titles, and an independent run (poplar-trie README) 0.43 vs 1.29 GiB on 14.1M titles and 2.68 vs 6.05 GiB on 39.5M UK URLs.
You need a dynamic (insert and erase at any time) string dictionary that also answers prefix queries such as autocompletion or longest-prefix routing, which hash maps cannot do.
Lookup latency close to std::unordered_map is acceptable: the independent run measured identical lookup times (0.27 us/key on Wikipedia titles, 0.51 vs 0.50 us on UK URLs).
Keys arrive in sorted or clustered order: on the README's sorted Wikipedia run it reads at 68 ns/key versus 174 ns for std::unordered_map.
You want a vendorable, header-only, MIT-licensed drop-in for a string set or map with on-disk serialization.
when_not_to_use: Raw speed is the goal: open-addressing hash maps beat it on random-order lookups and inserts (README: tsl::hopscotch_map 119.5 ns read and 240.6 ns insert with reserve vs 250.9 and 643.1 ns; independent run: robin_map 0.12 and dense_hash_map 0.14 us lookup vs 0.27).

Inserts dominate: htrie_map inserts slower than std::unordered_map in both independent datasets (0.60 vs 0.50 us/key on titles, 1.08 vs 0.67 on URLs), because each insert reallocs the bucket buffer and leaves periodically burst.

Memory must be minimal: succinct or compact tries use far less (poplar compact_bonsai_map 0.24 GiB vs 0.43 GiB on titles; JudySL 2.21 vs 2.68 GiB on URLs; static marisa-trie or xcdat smaller still) at the cost of slower lookups or no updates.
You need ordered iteration (keys inside a leaf are hashed, so iteration order is not lexicographic) or stable iterators across modifications.
Keys are not char (wchar_t, char16_t, char32_t are rejected at compile time) or exceed 65,535 bytes without raising the KeySizeT template parameter.

integration.dependencies: none (array-hash is vendored under include/tsl/array-hash; Boost.Test only for the test suite)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; README says tested with GCC 4.8.4, Clang 3.5.0 and Visual Studio 2015; CMake 3.10 for the exported tsl::hat_trie target
integration.platforms: any (portable C++; no SIMD or architecture-specific code)
integration.thread_safety: README: thread-safety and exception guarantees similar to STL containers (concurrent const reads OK, any writer needs external locking)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — API mirrors std::unordered_map, but there is no std::string key object (it.key() rebuilds one), value_type is not std::pair, every insert/emplace/erase invalidates all iterators, no allocator parameter, and iteration order differs

gotchas: Every modifying operation (insert, emplace, operator[], erase, clear) invalidates all iterators, not just those to the touched element.

Default hash is std::hash<std::string_view> only when compiled as C++17 or later; under C++11/14 it falls back to a byte-at-a-time FNV-1a, and the README reports CityHash64 gives about 20% faster reads, so pass a better hash functor on older standards (the published benchmark used CityHash64).
Memory comes from malloc/realloc and new with no allocator template parameter, so custom or shared-memory allocators are not supported (issue #59 asks how to use it with shared memory).

erase_prefix had crash bugs: issue #57 (iteration after erase_prefix, fixed August 2024) and issue #62 (equal_prefix_range on a fully erased prefix dereferenced a null bucket, fixed by commit ef3213d 'Bugfix on erase_prefix when erasing a full hash_node' in v0.7.1, November 2025, although the issue is still open); use 0.7.1 or newer. burst_threshold values of 65536 or more misbehaved before a clamp was added in August 2024 (issue #54).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over poplar-trie when lookup speed matters more than the last factor of memory (0.27 vs 0.68-1.02 us/key lookups for 0.43 vs 0.24-0.64 GiB in poplar's own run), and over marisa-trie, xcdat or darts-clone when the dictionary must accept inserts and erases after construction; those static tries are smaller but must be rebuilt to change.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's 2017 benchmark (public gist, GCC 6.3, -O3 -march=native, CityHash64 for every hash structure, libstdc++, Intel i5-5200u laptop), inserting and then reading 13.1M shuffled Wikipedia titles took 402 MiB versus 1247 MiB for std::unordered_map<std::string,int> and 1254 MiB for cedar::da, with reads at 251 ns/key (std::unordered_map 174, cedar::da 557), so it beats the standard map on memory only and other tries on speed; the gist times one pass per run (the README's best-of-20 is not in the code) and its std::unordered_map insert wrapper, map.insert({str, value}), copies each key twice, which inflates that baseline's insert time a little but not its memory or reads. An independent harness (kampersanda/dictionary_bench, g++ 7.3.0 -O3, Xeon E5-2680 v2) reproduced about 3x less memory than std::unordered_map with equal lookup time and slower inserts; no correctness bug was found behind the numbers.
status_note: Maintained at a slow pace (v0.7.1, last commit 2025-11-11, erase_prefix bug fixed in that release, one open PR removing the vtable pointer from nodes); MIT, header-only and portable, so it is easy to vendor.
